name: Hana Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head cashier at Delmar Market, a big supermarket on Harbour Road. I open at six forty, count the floats, set up the rota for the six tills and then I'm either on a till myself or fixing a problem somewhere, like a price that scans wrong or a customer who's upset about a coupon. I'm also the union rep for our shop, so people grab me in the break room with their contracts. What wears me out is the standing and the rush at five when everybody comes in at once.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and do you use any AI tools yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What do I like? Regulars, honestly. Customers think a cashier just scans things, but I know which of my older regulars need their bags packed and who's having a bad week. Mrs Okafor brings me a lemon cake every Christmas. I've been here since I left college at 19, so eight years, and I'm good at it. Fast, accurate, calm when it kicks off. That counts for something and I don't want it thrown away. Mostly I don't use any of the AI things, no. My phone does enough. Joel, my partner, drives a city bus and he teases me that I'd still use a paper diary if the shop let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've said for years: it's a gadget that scans a bit faster and that's about it. At work I'd tell the new girls not to panic when management waves some new software around, because half of it ends up in a drawer. Online I probably wouldn't say anything, I don't post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means very little for me. I'd carry on as head cashier, I earn well for the job and Joel and I have about eight months of rent and bills in the savings account. My worry is the same one as before, which is that Delmar keeps squeezing the rota and calls it efficiency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working my shifts and keep the union meetings going, first Tuesday of the month in the staff room. I'd put another few hundred a month into savings like I do now. I wouldn't touch any new tool unless they forced it on me, and then I'd ask the union to check it doesn't change our hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, really. A bit bored of the talk, if I'm honest. It's a relief if the whole thing turns out to be noise, because then I get to do the job I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your worry is the rota. What happened with the rota recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring head office cut two hours off every evening shift and said the self-checkouts covered it. Then the queues at the staffed tills got longer and customers took it out on us. We got the hours partly back after I took twelve signatures to the store manager, Dennis. That's the sort of thing I mean, it isn't AI, it's owners squeezing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the plateau lasts ten years, what's your life look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the same shop, maybe I'm the deputy manager if I ever put in for it. I'd like a flat of our own, so I'd keep saving toward a deposit. Nothing dramatic, and I'd be fine with that.

say: I'd tell colleagues it's a **gadget** that scans a bit faster, so there's no need to panic.
I'd warn the newer staff that new **software** often ends up forgotten in a drawer.
think: My job and my savings feel **secure**, so this changes very little for me.
My real worry is head office **squeezing** the rota, which has nothing to do with AI.
do: Keep working my shifts as head cashier and holding the monthly **union** meeting.
Keep adding a few hundred a month to **savings** towards a flat deposit.
Ask the union to check any new tool before it touches our **hours**.
feel: **Relieved** and a little bored of the hype.
S0.quote: I'd tell the new girls not to panic when management waves some new software around, because half of it ends up in a drawer.
fieldNote: Calm **because** the job and the cushion are solid, but the rota squeeze is an old pressure she brings unprompted.
She frames every change **through** the union and who benefits, not through the technology itself.

steps.text: Keep working six-forty openings as head cashier at Delmar
Put a few hundred a month towards a flat deposit
Have the union check any new software before it changes hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's more of the same story: machines doing what they can and the company keeping the savings. At work I'd start pushing in union meetings for a clause that says no one loses hours to software without talking to us first. Online I'd probably share the union's posts and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, it's a slow squeeze. My day is not much thinking work, it's people and scanning and packing, so the writing and booking side doesn't touch me. But the office above me does shrink, and head office will look at the shop and ask why we need six tills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make sure every cashier at Delmar is signed up to the union and I'd ask for a written agreement on rotas. I'd do the training they offer for the self-checkout supervisor role, if they pay for it, because that's the job that survives. I'd also add maybe five hundred a month to savings and hold off on buying the car we've been looking at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's on my mind when I'm lying in bed. I know I'm good and I know there are plenty of shops hiring, but I don't want to start again at a place where nobody knows me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually say to a cashier whose hours get cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit her down in the break room and show her the contract, then take her to Dennis with me. I'd also tell her to start looking at the other supermarkets on the ring road quietly, because there are jobs there. Loyalty only goes one way in a supermarket, so I'd tell every cashier at Delmar to look at the other shops quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do the supervisor training even though you avoid new tech. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. I avoid it when it's pushed on me for no reason. If it keeps me employed and the union has looked at it, I'll learn it, slowly and grumbling. I just won't pretend to love it.

say: I'd say machines do the work and the **company** keeps the savings.
I'd push a **union** clause so no one loses hours to software without a conversation.
think: My day is people and scanning, so the thinking-AI part barely **touches** me.
I expect head office to ask why we need six **tills**.
do: Sign every Delmar cashier up to the **union** and ask for rotas in writing.
Take the self-checkout **supervisor** training if the company pays for it.
Add about five hundred a month to **savings** and delay the car.
feel: **Uneasy**, especially lying awake, but confident I could find work nearby.
S1.quote: Loyalty only goes one way in a supermarket, so I'd tell every cashier at Delmar to look at the other shops quietly.
fieldNote: She **separates** the thinking tasks, which barely touch her, from the cuts to tills and hours, which she expects.
She admits **reluctantly** that she would learn new tools if they keep her job and the union has checked them.

steps.text: Sign up every cashier at Delmar to the union this spring
Train as self-checkout supervisor if the company pays
Save five hundred a month and delay buying the car

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disaster handed to us with no warning and somebody needs to answer for it. At work I'd call an emergency union meeting the first week. Online I'd actually post, which I never do, because the government has to hear from people like us before 2031 comes round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years of notice and then the tills go about three years after. Thinking AI doesn't hurt cashiers first, the robots do, but when robots get good that's my whole job: scanning, packing, restocking shelves. I'm anxious because everything I'm good at is exactly what they'd replace. I'm not sure what the human bit left over would even be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing is I'd stop spending and put every spare euro in savings, so the eight months becomes eleven or twelve. Second, I'd push the union and the other shops' unions to demand a notice period and retraining pay before any till is removed. Third, I'd go and learn something that needs hands and judgement, maybe a care course at the college, which I'd hate to say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panic, because I have money and there's Joel, but a tight chest. I keep seeing the tills at Delmar with nobody behind them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you do a care course when you love the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the shop could go and a care home needs people at night. It's hard work and I'd still be around people, which is the part I actually love. I'd rather choose a new line of work than be chosen, because everything I'm good at is exactly what a robot would replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big chains and the politicians who let them, not the machine. Delmar's owners would call it progress and bank the wage bill. If we'd had real rules on notice and retraining, this would be a different conversation.

say: I'd call it a **disaster** with no warning and demand someone answers for it.
I'd call an **emergency** union meeting and finally post online.
think: Robots reaching **hands-on** work is my whole job: scanning, packing and stocking.
I'm anxious but have **savings** and Joel, so it isn't panic.
do: Stop spending and stretch my **cushion** from eight months to a year.
Push for a **notice** period and paid retraining before any till is removed.
Enrol in a **care** course at the college for night work.
feel: **Anxious**, with a tight chest, picturing empty tills.
S2.quote: I'd rather choose a new line of work than be chosen, because everything I'm good at is exactly what a robot would replace.
fieldNote: She turns fear into **organising** first, then a private plan, and admits the care course reluctantly.
Blame goes to chains and **politicians** rather than the technology.

steps.text: Cut spending and move every spare euro into savings
Stretch savings from eight months to twelve
Demand paid retraining before any Delmar till is removed
Enrol in an evening care course at the college

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same warning, but five years. I'd say five years is long enough that we shouldn't be caught out, so no excuses. At work I'd get the union to open talks with Delmar head office now, while nobody's angry yet. Friends would hear me complain, I'm sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's still scary but it's survivable. By 2034 the tills are mostly robot work, but I'm 27 and that's seven years off, so I've got time to change. I'd feel the pressure less in the first couple of years because the thinking side doesn't touch the shop floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first year to finish a part-time diploma in something like healthcare assistant or retail management. I'd move up to deputy manager if the chance came, because management lasts longer than tills. And I'd keep saving and aim for the flat deposit anyway, because I don't want to put my whole life on hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit better than the two-year one, still uneasy underneath. Five years feels like a real chance, if people use it. I worry most won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would deputy manager give you that till work doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Staff to look after and a say in the rota. If robots take the till, somebody still has to run the floor and deal with the angry customers. Dennis says he's got fifty-odd staff and six managers, so there's room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the flat, would you still buy with that risk hanging over it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy smaller than I wanted, with a bigger deposit, so the payments stay low even if I'm working fewer hours. Joel agrees. I'd rather own a tiny flat outright than sweat over a bigger one if my hours at Delmar get cut.

say: I'd say five years is **long** enough that nobody should be caught out.
I'd get the union to open **talks** with head office while nobody is angry.
think: The **robots** come around 2034, and at 27 I have time to change.
The thinking side doesn't touch the shop floor, so the first couple of years feel **lighter**.
do: Finish a part-time **diploma**, maybe healthcare assistant or retail management.
Aim for **deputy** manager, because management lasts longer than tills.
Keep saving for a smaller **flat** with a bigger deposit.
feel: Slightly better than the two-year case, but **uneasy** that most people won't use the time.
S3.quote: I'd rather own a tiny flat outright than sweat over a bigger one if my hours at Delmar get cut.
fieldNote: Her **anxiety** eases because time converts into concrete plans, with management as the safe harbour.
She is **willing** to buy smaller to keep payments low if hours get cut.

steps.text: Finish a part-time retail management diploma in the first year
Apply for deputy manager at Delmar when it opens
Save a bigger deposit for a smaller flat
Buy the flat smaller so payments stay low

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'd say it's not for me to panic about. At work I'd tell people to keep an eye on it, but not to throw away good jobs now. I'd bring it up at union meetings once a year so it doesn't get forgotten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is a lot of life. By 2039 I'll be 40, and there'll be robots in the shops, but I could be a manager or in some other field by then. It makes me less worried than the others, and more annoyed, because people will ignore it until it's late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Delmar and go for deputy manager in the next couple of years. I'd save for the flat and think about kids a bit later than planned, if things look shaky. And I'd probably try one AI thing, just to see what it is, Ten years is long enough that avoiding AI isn't a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish. It feels like a weather forecast, something you plan around rather than fear. Though I know I'm good at pushing things away until they land on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might try AI. What would make you actually do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the union ran a session and I could ask silly questions in a room with friends. I don't want to be told to try it alone with a screen. A Tuesday evening in the staff room, tea and biscuits, I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change your plans about having kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Joel and I both want them, probably around thirty-two. I'd want me or him in a secure job by then, so I'd be careful about picking something that lasts. That's what ten years gives me, a choice.

say: I'd tell colleagues to **watch** it but not throw away good jobs now.
I'd raise it at the **union** once a year so it isn't forgotten.
think: By 2039 I'll be 40, and I could be a **manager** or in another field.
People will ignore it until it's **late**, which annoys me.
do: Go for **deputy** manager at Delmar within the next couple of years.
Save for a **flat** and plan kids a little later if things look shaky.
Try one AI tool at a **union** session with colleagues.
feel: **Calm-ish**, like a weather forecast, though she knows she pushes things away until they land.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough that avoiding AI isn't a plan.
fieldNote: Time turns the issue from fear into **planning**, and she admits her habit of avoiding new technology.
She would only try AI in a group **setting**, which says a lot about how she learns.

steps.text: Apply for deputy manager at Delmar within two years
Attend a union evening session to try one AI tool
Keep working tills and save for the flat deposit
Time having children for around thirty-two with secure work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. Nobody has time to organise, the government hasn't got a plan, and the shops would just rip out tills the way they ripped out the pay phones. What would help is a promise in writing, a notice period, paid retraining and the union at the table before a single till goes. And honest talk from head office, because we always hear it last.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me get told it's all about learning to code or use apps, as if cashiers are lazy. We're not. We're fast, careful and good with people, and that should count when they decide who gets retrained and who gets pushed out.

headlineQuote: Customers think a cashier just scans things, but I know which of my older regulars need their bags packed and who's having a bad week.
portrait: **Hana** is a 27-year-old head cashier and union rep at Delmar Market, eight years in, well paid, with about eight months saved.
She is **progressive** and blames chains and politicians for any cuts, not the machines themselves.
She avoids new technology and has never used **AI**, but would learn it in a group if the union backed it.
Her mood moves from calm in the plateau to **anxious** when AGI is near, easing as the warning grows.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** case, because nobody has time to organise and tills would vanish quickly.
whatWouldHelp: A **written** notice period, paid retraining and the union at the table before any till goes.
